poiCOOP-desc:
The lithium of the Andes is mined by those who live on top of it. When the Great Mistake drove the foreign companies out of the old Andean mines, their workers and the indigenous communities that held the land refused to leave. They kept the pumps running, pooled their tools and their claims, and sold what they dug to whoever could still pay. The Cooperativa Minera de Lima grew out of that refusal, and today it is one of the largest mining enterprises in the world.

It belongs to its members. Every miner, every community and every district that joins holds a share and a vote, and the Cooperativa's delegates answer to {{poiCOOP004|an assembly}} rather than to investors. Its heart is the {{poiCOOP001|Casino Obrero Minero}} in Lima, once a workers' club and canteen, now its headquarters, its exchange and its bank. From there it runs {{poiCOOP002|the numbered mining districts it owns outright}} and buys from {{poiCOOP003|the free districts that sell through it}}.

Lithium is its lifeblood, with rare earths, copper, iron and coal beside it, and its output is one of the pillars on which the Andean Compact rests. The two depend on each other completely. Nobody in Lima passes a mining law the Cooperativa has not read first, and the Cooperativa has never forgotten that the Compact's armies, such as they are, {{poiCOOP005|stand between its mines and Brazil}}.
poiCOOP001-desc:
Every old Andean mining town had its casino obrero, the workers' club where miners ate, drank, argued and organised. The one in Lima became something more. During the Dark Age it was where the mining communities met to fix prices and settle disputes, and the habit stuck.

Today the Casino Obrero Minero is the Cooperativa's headquarters and its greatest asset. Lithium contracts are signed in its halls, its members' savings are held in its vaults, and its trading floor sets prices that buyers on four continents follow. The canteen is still there, and the cheapest meal in the building is still the one served to miners.
poiCOOP002-desc:
The Cooperativa owns its core mines outright, and names them the way the first surveyors did: by letter and number. The great salt flats and pit mines of Distritos Mineros A3, C2 and C4 produce most of its lithium, and each is run by an elected district council that sends delegates to Lima.

The districts are proud, competitive and suspicious of one another. C4, the largest, has long argued that it deserves a larger say. A3 and C2 answer that a vote is a vote. The assembly has settled the question the same way for decades, and C4 has grumbled about it for just as long.
poiCOOP003-desc:
Not every mine in the Andes belongs to the Cooperativa. The Distritos Mineros Libres are the free districts: community mines, family claims and small cooperatives of their own that have never joined, but sell through Lima because nobody else offers a fair price and a safe road to market.

The arrangement suits both sides, most of the time. The free districts keep their independence, and the Cooperativa keeps their output flowing through its exchange. Whenever prices fall, however, some in the assembly ask why the free districts should enjoy the Cooperativa's protection without sharing its obligations.
poiCOOP004-desc:
The Cooperativa is governed by its assembly, where delegates from every member district and community meet in the great hall of the Casino Obrero. Each holds one vote, whatever the size of the mine behind it. Delegates serve short terms and can be recalled, and the assembly elects the officers who run the Cooperativa between sessions.

The great argument of the present assembly is automation. The engineers and the younger delegates want the machines that would let the mines dig deeper and faster with fewer people. The elders and the communities that hold the land answer that the Cooperativa exists to keep people working on their own ground, and that a mine run by machines is just a foreign company with a different name.
poiCOOP005-desc:
Like every great interest in the Andean Compact, the Cooperativa keeps its own armed force. The Guardia Minera guards the districts, the roads and the trains that carry lithium to the coast, and it answers to the assembly rather than to Lima's generals. It is well paid and well equipped, and it does not deploy far from the mines.

The Compact's army reviews count the Guardia among the forces it could call upon in a war. The Guardia's officers have never been asked, and are in no hurry to find out what they would answer.
